---
title: "Adopt the Pet"
---

::: {.ao-story}
In a corner of the Kennel a small pet blinks at you. It is a small model that runs on your own machine, costs nothing to feed and forgets things easily, and the kennel master, asked a plain question, admits it is no Beast. Even a small helper needs a lead before it goes near anything that matters. First, bring it home and find out how much it can hold in its head.
:::

::: {.quest-dialog}
- **Goal:** you will run a small local model with Ollama, give it enough context, and point OpenCode at it.
- **Before you start:** [Know Your Gear](../basecamp/know-your-gear.html) and [Save Point](../crypt/shield-of-undo.html); a laptop with about 16 GB of memory; a terminal; roughly 5 GB of free disk. OpenCode is an open-source coding agent (a program that runs a model and its tools) that can use local models.
- **Time:** about 20 minutes. Everything stays on your machine.
:::

A local model runs on your own computer, so prompts stay there and use costs nothing. Use one when your data agreement rules out hosted models, or when you want to try an agent without paying. You need this lesson now because the next lessons assume you can run a model without sending data out. A small local model holds less in mind and makes more mistakes than a hosted one, so check its answers before you rely on them.

## 1. Install Ollama and fetch a model

If you already installed Ollama and OpenCode on the OpenCode route, you have done steps 1 to 3. Go to step 4.

Ollama is a program that downloads and runs models on your own computer.

```bash
curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh     # macOS and Linux
ollama pull qwen3:4b                              # about 2.5 GB
ollama run qwen3:4b "Say hello in one sentence."
```

`qwen3:4b` is one example of a small model that Ollama lists with tool support (the model can ask the agent to run actions such as reading a file). Model names change quickly, so check the "tools" badge on the model's page at ollama.com/library. The `ollama run` command prints a short greeting from the model. Run `ollama ps` (lists the loaded models) in a second terminal while it runs to see what loaded and whether it fits your RAM (ordinary memory).

WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux) users: run the Linux commands inside your WSL terminal, and check each tool's current docs if one fails.

## 2. Set the context length

The context length (also called the context window: how much text the model can see at once) defaults to **4k tokens** (a token is a chunk of text, roughly a word or part of one) in Ollama on machines with under 24 GiB of video memory (VRAM, the memory on the graphics card or shared with it). That includes a 16 GB laptop. Agents and coding tools need **at least 64k**; OpenCode requires 64k or higher. The server is the background process that answers requests from tools such as OpenCode. Set the context length when you start it. Run this in a separate terminal and leave that terminal open:

```bash
OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=64000 ollama serve
```

If the Ollama desktop app is already running, open its settings and set the context length slider to 64k instead; `ollama serve` would clash with the running server. Then check what loaded with `ollama ps`. A bigger context needs more memory. Look at the PROCESSOR column: a model that spills onto the CPU (the main processor) runs slower than one that stays on the GPU.

## 3. Point OpenCode at it

Install OpenCode, then start it with `opencode` in a project folder. Type `/models` inside it (a `/command` is typed inside the running tool) and pick your Ollama model. Ollama needs no `/connect`. A working screen shows a prompt box where you type; your first message gets an answer from the local model.

```bash
curl -fsSL https://opencode.ai/v2/install | bash
```

If the install command errors, check the current OpenCode docs for your version.

OpenCode finds Ollama at `http://127.0.0.1:11434` automatically, so this step is optional. To spell the address out, create `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` (the global OpenCode config file) with this content:

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "providers": {
    "ollama": { "settings": { "baseURL": "http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1" } }
  }
}
```

## 4. Limit what the agent may do

OpenCode's default policy is **allow everything**, except reading `.env` files, which it asks about. Shell commands run with your user's authority, and the shell is not a sandbox (nothing confines a command to one folder, so a command can touch any file you can). Each rule says `allow` (run without asking), `ask` (prompt you first) or `deny` (never run). A safer start puts the ask-everything rule first, then allows only what you trust. A catch-all rule placed later overrides the rules above it, because the last matching rule wins. Add this to the same `opencode.json` file, next to the `providers` block from step 3. **Rules are checked in order and the last match wins:**

```json
{
  "permissions": [
    { "action": "*", "resource": "*", "effect": "ask" },
    { "action": "shell", "resource": "git status *", "effect": "allow" },
    { "action": "shell", "resource": "git push *", "effect": "deny" }
  ]
}
```

## Other small models to try

Mistral publishes open-weight models (models whose trained weights you can download and run yourself) that Ollama lists with tool support. Apache 2.0 is a permissive open-source licence that allows commercial use.

- **`ministral-3`:** 3B (3.0 GB), 8B (6.0 GB) and 14B (9.1 GB) sizes, Apache 2.0.
- **`mistral-small`:** 24B (14 GB), Apache 2.0.

A 24B model has about eight times the parameters of a 3B one and needs far more memory, so check `ollama ps` after loading.

## A built-in model on newer Macs

Recent Macs ship a small on-device model (it runs on the Mac itself) with the operating system, and developers call it through Apple's Foundation Models framework. Availability depends on whether your device and region support Apple Intelligence, and the model can take a while to download after you turn that on. It suits summarising, extracting and classifying text. It may struggle with basic math, code and logical reasoning.

## Lore

*Further reading. Optional.*

- [ministral-3](https://ollama.com/library/ministral-3): Ollama library, docs. Why read: it lists the sizes, context length, tool support and licence of a small Mistral model you can pull instead of a Qwen one.
- [OpenCode](https://docs.ollama.com/integrations/opencode): Ollama, docs. Why read: it is the vendor guide to running OpenCode against a local Ollama model, including the context length it needs. It still shows older OpenCode install commands, so check the OpenCode docs too.
- [Providers](https://opencode.ai/docs/providers/): OpenCode, docs. Why read: it shows how to connect Ollama or an OpenAI-compatible gateway in the current config format.
- [Config](https://opencode.ai/docs/config/): OpenCode, docs. Why read: it lists where `opencode.json` lives and how global and project files override each other.
- [Permissions](https://opencode.ai/docs/permissions/): OpenCode, docs. Why read: it explains how to control what the agent may do, which matters more with a small local model.
- [Foundation Models updates](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/updates/foundationmodels): Apple, docs. Why read: it lists the changes to Apple's on-device model by date, including which OS versions change the model.
- [anomalyco/opencode](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode): GitHub, repo. Why read: it is the source and release list, useful when the docs and your installed version disagree.
:::
